transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2025-08-11
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~46 minutes
- Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood Solutions), Aisha (VerdantAI Head ML), Ben (VerdantAI Platform), Claire (CTO), Evan (ML Eng)

Summary: VerdantAI is evaluating Redwood for a 4-week POC to validate production performance for a user-facing assistant: they want p95 latency under 200ms for short chat (<=2k tokens), embeddings under 100ms, and the ability to handle spikes up to ~200 concurrent requests. Key constraints: data residency, SOC 2 compliance, and platform integration with their Kubernetes-based infra. They prefer reserved GPUs for predictable baseline and a burst pool for peaks, with automatic fallback to smaller quantized variants.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh, appreciate you setting aside time. Quick intro - I'm Samira, AE at Redwood, with Liam on the tech side. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Aisha: Hi Samira, doing well. Thanks. I'm Aisha, head of ML at VerdantAI. We've got Ben, Claire, and Evan on our side.
[00:12] Liam: Hey, hi, team. Quick agenda: scoping success criteria, dig into workloads, runbook for a POC (reserved capacity + burst), and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:20] Claire: Yep that's fine. We want to get into specifics - costs, how the burst works, and what happens on saturation.

[00:35] Ben: To give context - our prod assistant serves customers live on our web app. Typical steady-state is around 25-40 qps for short chat requests, but we have occasional spikes during morning syncs where it goes to 180-220 concurrent requests for ~10-20 minutes. Most requests are short, avg token output ~120 tokens, but we also have longer contexts for certain power users.
[00:56] Evan: Also we run embeddings for search updates hourly, that's a background job with bulk requests, and it's latency-sensitive up to a point - ideally embeddings finishes within a minute for a batch of 10k docs, but for the POC we'll scope only the online part and a small embeddings subset.

[01:15] Diego: Got it. Do you have traces or histograms of QPS and sequence length distribution we can use to size the POC?
[01:22] Ben: Yes, we can share traces. We'll need guidance on what slices you want - tails, percentiles, peak periods.
[01:30] Liam: Perfect. For sizing, two knobs we typically consider: reserved GPUs to cover steady throughput, and burst pool - ephemeral capacity for spikes. For the POC we usually recommend reserving enough to handle sustained 40-60 qps at your target latency and enabling a burst pool sized to handle your 200-concurrent spikes for short windows.
[01:53] Aisha: Curious - is the burst just spinning up more dedicated GPUs or do you fall back to hosted multi-tenant? Security-wise we need data-in-transit and at-rest encryption and we don't want requests routed off our VPC for the POC.
[02:08] Liam: Good question. For Redwood Dedicated + Private combos you can have a reserved pool inside your VPC and a burst pool that's also within the same private deployment; it doesn't route to multi-tenant hosted unless you opt-in. The burst is typically additional reserved hardware we can temporarily uncap for you; for short POC spikes we can also serve with quantized model variants which increase throughput per GPU.
[02:33] Samira: To add - we offer two burst patterns: warm standby (pre-warmed small pool, low-cost) and elastic spin-up (cold start but faster in our infra). For SOC2 environments we recommend warm standby for critical endpoints to avoid routing outside the VPC.

[02:50] Claire: Okay, makes sense. Performance tradeoffs are important: if we use quantized model for burst, what's the expected latency and quality delta?
[02:59] Liam: Typically, for 8-bit quantization we see 1.8-2x throughput gain and a small drop in some sensitive evals - depending on your prompts. For chat short responses, many customers don't notice a quality regression, but for long-context or instruction-sensitive outputs you may see differences. We can run A/B evals in the POC.

[03:20] Ben: On SLOs - our product team wants p95 end-to-end under 200ms for chat, and embeddings p95 under 100ms. Are those realistic on commodity A100s or do we need more specialized hardware?
[03:31] Liam: For short chat with optimized kernels and batching tuned, hitting p95 ~150ms on A100s for the model class you're targeting is achievable if you keep sequence lengths low and set batching windows aggressively. Embeddings are often sub-100ms per request on V100/A100 depending on model size. We'll confirm with bench runs.

[03:50] Aisha: We briefly looked at your docs. Can you outline a POC timeline? We have a shipping window so need to compress to 4 weeks if possible.
[03:58] Samira: Typical POC cadence: Week 0 - setup + security review + dataset and traces exchanged; Week 1 - bench script + baseline runs (engineer-to-engineer); Week 2 - tuning (batching, autoscale thresholds, quantization profiles); Week 3 - load spike tests + fallback validation; Week 4 - analysis, metrics review, and decision/contract. We can compress some steps if VerdantAI provides traces and credentials up front.

[04:25] Evan: For benchmarks, we'll want to run our real request traces rather than synthetic. Is that supported?
[04:30] Liam: Yes - we can replay traces through the POC environment. We ask that you scrub PII if any, or we can provide guidance for redaction. Replay gives more accurate KV-cache hit patterns and batching characteristics.

[04:45] Ben: About fallback policies - what are options when the system is saturating? We don't want cascading failures if GPUs max out.
[04:52] Diego: We typically implement a multi-layer fallback: 1) prefer queuing with backpressure and token-level timeouts, 2) automatic model fallback to a smaller/quantized variant if latency breaches a threshold, 3) region or tier fallback (route to a lower-cost hosted instance) as a last resort, and 4) circuit-breaker to return a graceful degraded response. You can configure thresholds per route.

[05:15] Claire: Circuit-breaker is critical. Can we define our own fallback response for degraded mode? e.g., a shorter reply or canned message?
[05:21] Liam: Yes, you can define structured fallbacks, and Redwood supports function-tool-call-style fallbacks so the app can decide how to render degraded content.

[05:30] Aisha: Cost question: how do you price reserved vs burst? Do you do hourly billing for burst or a fixed add-on?
[05:36] Samira: Reserved is a monthly commit (we prorate for the POC). Burst can be either metered hourly or via a prepaid burst pool - for POCs we often do a capped metered burst so you only pay for what you use. We'll include both options in the pricing sheet.

[05:50] Ben: Any limit on burst frequency? Our spikes are short but frequent during day start and product launches occasionally.
[05:55] Liam: We set burst policies with cooldowns and quotas - you can set max bursts per hour/day to control cost and avoid noisy neighbor effects. For POC we'll advise a conservative cap and adjust if needed.

[06:08] Evan: How about autoscaling times? If we rely on spin-up, what's realistic latency to get more GPUs?
[06:13] Diego: Elastic spin-up is generally 2-5 minutes depending on provisioning and image pulls; warm standby is effectively immediate (<30s) since instances are pre-warmed. For user-facing endpoints we recommend warm standby for low p95.

[06:26] Aisha: For the POC we probably want a baseline of reserved 4 A100 GPUs, warm standby of 2, and the ability to burst to 8 additional GPUs for very short peaks. Is that a reasonable starting point?
[06:38] Liam: Yes, that sounds fine as a starting configuration. We'll run initial bench to validate. If your typical request sizes are small, we might be able to move some of the load into fewer GPUs by increasing batch windows and quantization.

[06:52] Ben: We also want to test failure modes - what happens if our network pegs or there's a region outage? Can we failover to another region or to Redwood-hosted?
[06:59] Diego: Yes, we support cross-region routing and automatic failover policies. For Private deployments, cross-region failover still stays in your private VPC constructs if you set up inter-region private peering. If you need absolute isolation, we can instead use local redundancy and fallback to a read-only degraded response.

[07:20] Claire: On security: we need SOC2 docs, SSO integration (SAML/Okta), and HSM/KMS support for keys. Also audit logs for all inference calls for compliance audits.
[07:29] Samira: We will share the SOC2 pack and our security whitepaper. Redwood Private supports KMS integration and audit logs; SSO and RBAC are supported via SAML. We'll attach the diagrams showing network flow (VPC peering, private endpoints).

[07:45] Aisha: Great. For success criteria for the POC, let's propose: 1) demonstrate p95 chat latency <=200ms for steady-state traffic, 2) handle spike to 200 concurrent with p95 degradation no more than 2x baseline or graceful fallback, 3) embedding batch throughput meets our hourly window for the sampled dataset, 4) security checklist passes (SOC2 + SSO).

[08:05] Samira: That's a crisp set. We'll add measurable thresholds and logging we can instrument. We'll also run quality regressions on a prompt set you provide.

[08:14] Ben: For the benchmark script, what metrics will you capture? We need to see p50/p95/p99 latencies, token-level cost, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and KV-cache hit rates.

[08:23] Liam: We'll capture all of those. We'll surface them in a perf dashboard and share a CSV/retrospective. Also we'll include suggestions for batching and quantization to hit your targets.

[08:34] Evan: About model variants - can you automatically fall back from a 7B float model to a 7B quantized model? Is that just a flag?

[08:40] Diego: It's a configuration: we test model compatibility first in onboarding. The runtime supports pinning variants and automatic fallbacks. We'll validate with your model family to ensure behavior is consistent.

[08:52] Claire: Timeline check - if we start week of Aug 18 with traces shared by Aug 15, can we complete the 4-week POC by mid-September?

[08:59] Samira: Yes, that's feasible. Action items: we'll send the contract and pricing, Liam will send the bench scripts, and VerdantAI to share traces and confirm success criteria by Aug 14 so we can provision resources for Aug 18.

[09:15] Aisha: Sounds good. A couple of minor items: can we get an estimate of expected monthly cost if we go to production with the proposed config? Even ballpark numbers would help our finance team.

[09:24] Samira: We'll provide ballpark monthly estimates for multiple profiles: reserved-only, reserved + warm standby, and reserved + elastic metered burst. That'll be in the pricing sheet.

[09:32] Ben: One more - can you do an engineer-to-engineer run where Liam pairs with Evan to run the replay? Better to have that handoff during week 1.

[09:40] Liam: Absolutely - I'll block time and include the bench run instructions.

[09:45] Claire: Okay, that's all from me.
[09:47] Samira: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items we talked about. Recap of next steps: pricing + security pack, bench script, traces, and schedule the engineer bench week of Aug 18.

[09:59] Aisha: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:01] Samira: Thanks all, bye.

--- End transcript ---

Notes on transcription quality: Some brand names may be slightly off (Redwood Dedicated sometimes heard as 'Redwood Dedicate'), and there are minor filler words and overlaps as typical in real calls.
